groups.label: Moral Inquiries and Challenge
groups.summary: Commentary traces the evolution of moral stages and of Socrates himself across the early dialogue, moving from traditional precepts of justice to the sharp challenges of Glaucon and Adeimantus, who demand proof of justice's inherent worth beyond external rewards.
groups.rationale: These entries all focus on the dialectical progression of defining justice and the role of the interlocutors in Books I and II.

groups.label: Civic Structure and Guardians
groups.summary: Socrates establishes the city–soul analogy and transitions from a basic settlement to a luxurious state, requiring a dedicated guardian class organized under strict communal living and legitimated by the myth of the metals.
groups.rationale: These nodes cover the socio-political architecture of the ideal republic, specifically the state-individual analogy, social classes, and guardian discipline.

groups.label: Guardian Education and Culture
groups.summary: The education of the guardians demands rigorous censorship of theological myth and poetic imitation, alongside the purification of musical modes and physical gymnastics in service of psychic harmony.
groups.rationale: These items directly detail the cultural, musical, literary, and physical curriculum established for the education of the guardian class.

groups.label: Degeneration and Regime Metrics
groups.summary: Commentary analyzes the degeneration of the ideal city into timocracy and oligarchy, framing this sequence as an order of thought rather than historical fact and culminating in mathematical calculations contrasting the happiness of the king and tyrant.
groups.rationale: These entries center on Books VIII and IX, analyzing the decline of constitutional forms, their character types, historical validity, and the ultimate measure of the tyrant.

groups.label: Cicero's Imitations of Plato
groups.summary: Cicero adapts Platonic concepts such as the vision of Er in the Somnium Scipionis and grounds his ideal state in Roman history, but his rhetorical style and unoriginal philosophy fall short of Plato's art.
groups.rationale: This entry stands apart as a retrospective commentary evaluating Cicero's later Roman adaptations and stylistic inferiority compared to Plato.
